sections.heading: Article 324: what the Election Commission is and who sits in it

blocks.title: Basic nature
items: The Election Commission of India (ECI) is a permanent, independent body created directly by the Constitution (a constitutional body, not a statutory body).
Art 324 gives it 'superintendence, direction and control' (full charge) of elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, the office of President and the office of Vice-President.
It is an all-India body: the same Commission serves both the Centre and the States.
It does NOT conduct elections to panchayats and municipalities. These are conducted by the State Election Commission (Art 243K and Art 243ZA, added by the 73rd and 74th Amendments, 1992).
It also does NOT conduct the election of the Lok Sabha Speaker or the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman. The members of the House elect them inside the House.

Rule

The Commission has no large staff of its own. When it asks, the President and the Governors must provide the staff needed for elections
blocks.note: The Constitution does not fix the number of Election Commissioners. 'Three members' is the present practice, not a constitutional rule.

blocks.title: What the ECI does NOT do
items: It does not decide election disputes. Election petitions go to the High Court (Art 329 and the Representation of the People Act (RP Act), 1951). Disputes about the President's and Vice-President's elections go to the Supreme Court (Art 71).
It does not decide how many Lok Sabha seats each State gets. That is fixed by Art 81 and Art 82 and the Delimitation Commission.
It cannot de-register (cancel the registration of) a party for breaking the RP Act, 1951, because the law gives it no such power (see Political parties).
It cannot itself dismiss a government officer. Officers on election duty work under its control, and it can ask the government to act against them.
It does not conduct elections to co-operative societies or local bodies.

The ECI first became multi-member on 16 October 1989 (by the President's order, not by any Act). It went back to a single member in January 1990, and became multi-member again in October 1993. The Constitution does not fix the number of ECs.

The Model Code of Conduct (MCC) is not backed by any law and starts from the day the schedule is announced. For a breach, the ECI can warn or censure, but cannot disqualify or fine.

subcards.summary: How India's elections are run: Articles 324–329, election laws, delimitation and reforms.
at_a_glance: Art 324 to 329 are in Part XV of the Constitution. Art 329A was repealed (removed). Art 323B allows election tribunals
18 years, since the 61st Amendment (passed 1988, in force from 28 March 1989)
Representation of the People (RP) Act 1950 covers seats and voters' lists. RP Act 1951 covers conducting elections, disqualifications and disputes
File an election petition (a case challenging the result) in the High Court within 45 days. Appeal goes to the Supreme Court

₹25,000 for general candidates and ₹12,500 for SC and ST candidates. A loser forfeits (loses) it if his votes are not more than one-sixth of valid votes
In big states: ₹95 lakh for Lok Sabha and ₹40 lakh for Assembly candidates (2022). There is no limit on political parties

blocks.title: Articles on elections (Part XV)
head: Article
What it says
Remember
rows: Superintendence, direction and control of elections (full charge of running them) is given to the Election Commission
Covers Parliament, State Legislatures, President and Vice-President. Not panchayats or municipalities (State Election Commission does those)
One general electoral roll (voters' list) for every territorial constituency. No one can be left out of it, or claim a special roll, only because of religion, race, caste or sex
Ended the British-era 'separate electorates' (separate voters' lists for each community), which had led to partition
Elections to Lok Sabha and State Assemblies are on the basis of adult suffrage (every adult citizen can vote)
Age 18. A law can disqualify a voter only for non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime, or corrupt or illegal practice. Literacy is NOT a ground
Parliament can make laws on all election matters: electoral rolls, delimitation of constituencies and other matters
Parliament used this to make the RP Acts 1950 and 1951 and the Delimitation Acts
A State Legislature can make laws on elections to its own legislature (for example, electoral rolls)
Only on matters where Parliament has not made a law. A state law can only fill gaps in Parliament's law, never override it
A law on delimitation of constituencies or allotment of seats cannot be questioned in any court
So orders of the Delimitation Commission (the body that draws constituency boundaries) are final
An election to Parliament or a State Legislature can be questioned only by an election petition, as the law provides
So courts do not stop an election midway; it can be challenged only after the result (N.P. Ponnuswami case, 1952)
Placed disputes about the election of the Prime Minister and the Lok Sabha Speaker outside the power of the courts
Inserted by the 39th Amendment (1975); repealed by the 44th Amendment (1978)

blocks.title: Related Articles
head: Article
Point
rows: Art 81 and Art 170 fix the size of Lok Sabha and State Assemblies. Art 170: an Assembly has at most 500 and at least 60 members. Art 81: seats are given to states so that the population per seat is, as far as practicable, the same in all states. This rule does not apply to a state with a population of 6 million or less
Readjustment (re-fixing) of Lok Sabha seats and constituencies after each census
Seats reserved for SCs and STs in Lok Sabha (Art 330) and State Assemblies (Art 332)
Qualifications to be an MP: Indian citizen, oath, minimum age, and other conditions Parliament prescribes. No educational qualification is prescribed
Disputes on the election of the President or Vice-President are decided by the Supreme Court (not the High Court)

Allows a legislature to set up a tribunal (special court-like body) for election disputes. No such tribunal has ever been set up. In the L. Chandra Kumar case (1997) the Supreme Court struck down the clause that kept courts out, so an appeal from any such tribunal would go to the High Court
Panchayat and municipal elections are run by the State Election Commission. Art 243-O (panchayats) and Art 243ZG (municipalities) stop courts from interfering, just like Art 329

Delimitation means fixing the boundaries of constituencies. It keeps the population of constituencies roughly equal, so that every vote has about the same value ('one person, one vote, one value'). If one constituency has far fewer people, a vote there counts for more.

sections.heading: Parties: meaning, types and party systems

blocks.text: A political party is a voluntary group of people who share the same political views and try to win power by constitutional (lawful) means.

blocks.title: Parties and the Constitution
items: The original Constitution did not mention political parties at all.
Citizens form parties using the freedom to form associations — Article 19(1)(c).
The words 'political party' first came into the Constitution through the 52nd Amendment (1985), which added the Tenth Schedule (anti-defection law).
Even so, parties are called an 'extra-constitutional growth': they grew up outside the Constitution and were not created by it.

blocks.text: See the card 'Anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule)' for who decides disqualification of a member — the Speaker or Chairman of the House, not the President.

head: Type
Aim
Place on the spectrum
rows: Go back to the old social, economic and political order
Keep things as they are (status quo)
Overthrow existing institutions and set up a new order
blocks.note: Indian examples (Laxmikanth): CPI and CPI(M) are leftist, Congress is centrist, BJP is rightist.

blocks.title: Three party systems
head: System
Meaning
Example
rows: Only the ruling party exists; no opposition allowed
Former USSR and East European communist countries

blocks.title: Useful terms
items: Hung Parliament (or hung assembly): no single party wins a majority of seats.
Manifesto: a party's written list of the programmes and promises it will carry out.
A. Lawrence Lowell called political parties 'brokers of ideas'.

Functions of parties: put up candidates, offer different policies for voters to choose from, shape public opinion, form the government or act as opposition. Drawing constituency boundaries (delimitation) is NOT their job — the Delimitation Commission does it.

sections.heading: Indian party system and its history

blocks.title: Features of the Indian party system (Laxmikanth)
head: Feature
What it means
rows: India has the largest number of parties in the world. Causes: huge size, diverse society, universal adult franchise from the start, its type of political process. Result: hung Parliaments and coalition governments are common.
Congress dominated for a long time. Rajni Kothari called it the 'one party dominance system' or 'Congress system'. India was never a one-party system in law.
Only the BJP and the two communist parties (CPI, CPI(M)) have a clear ideology; most others are close to each other and mainly seek power.
People know a party by its leader more than by its manifesto (its list of promises). In short: 'political personalities rather than political parties'.
Many parties are based on religion, caste, language, culture or race (for example Shiromani Akali Dal, Shiv Sena, BSP). Lok Satta Party is not usually cited as such a party.
Many regional parties rule states and now matter at the Centre through coalitions.
Splits and defections rose sharply after the fourth general elections (1967).
Since the first elections, a strong and united national opposition has appeared only for short periods ('in flashes'), not all the time.
blocks.note: No Indian law makes regular elections inside a party compulsory.

blocks.title: Phases of the party system
head: Period
Feature

head: Provision
Subject

Registration of political parties with the Election Commission

items: A party applies to the Election Commission within 30 days of its formation.

Its memorandum (constitution) must promise true faith and allegiance to the Constitution of India and to socialism, secularism and democracy, and to uphold the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India. (Federalism is not in this list.)

Indian National Congress v Institute of Social Welfare (2002): the Supreme Court held that the Election Commission has no general power to cancel (de-register) a registered party, even if the party breaks these promises. There are only three exceptions: (1) the party got registration by fraud; (2) the Central Government has declared the party unlawful; or (3) the party itself removes these promises from its memorandum.

blocks.title: National party — any ONE of these routes
head: Route
Condition

2% of all Lok Sabha seats (11 of 543), AND these members are elected from at least 3 different states
Recognised as a state party in 4 states

8% of total valid votes in the state (Lok Sabha or assembly election) — no seat needed
blocks.note: Worked examples: in a 75-seat assembly, 3% of 75 is 2.25, which is less than 3, so the party needs 3 seats. Andhra Pradesh has 25 Lok Sabha seats, so winning 1 Lok Sabha seat there is enough.

items: If rival groups of a recognised party each claim the party's name and symbol, the Election Commission decides which group is the real party, under Paragraph 15 of the Symbols Order. Here it acts like a court (quasi-judicial authority).

subcards.title: Anti-defection law (Tenth Schedule)
subcards.summary: When an MP or MLA loses the seat for switching parties, and who decides.
at_a_glance: 52nd Amendment Act, 1985 (Rajiv Gandhi was Prime Minister)
Art 101, 102, 190 and 191 (rules on vacating seats and on disqualification)
Members of Parliament and of State Legislatures: party members, independents and nominated members
Merger, when two-thirds of the legislature party agree
Presiding officer of the House (the Speaker or the Chairman). The Schedule gives no time-limit for the decision.
Kihoto Hollohan case (1992): the presiding officer's decision can be examined by the courts (judicial review)

sections.heading: What defection is, and how the law grew

items: Defection means a legislator leaving the party on whose ticket he was elected and joining another. Other names: 'floor crossing', 'carpet crossing', 'party hopping'.
After the 4th general election (1967), the Congress party's dominance declined and defections rose sharply. Factions, splits and defections in parties increased noticeably.
'Aya Ram Gaya Ram' (came Ram, went Ram): from Gaya Lal, an MLA of Haryana, who changed parties several times in one day in 1967.
The 52nd Amendment gave political parties a place in the Constitution for the first time. The words 'political party' entered the Constitution through the Tenth Schedule.
Besides adding the Tenth Schedule, the 52nd Amendment changed Art 101, 102, 190 and 191 (vacating of seats and disqualification of MPs and MLAs).
The Constitution originally had 8 Schedules. The Tenth Schedule was added later, by the 52nd Amendment Act, 1985.

items.what: 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram' episode in Haryana (Gaya Lal)
First resolution on defection in the 4th Lok Sabha, moved by Pendekanti Venkatasubbaiah (a private member's resolution, 11 August 1967)
items.detail: It led to a Committee on Defections chaired by Home Minister Y.B. Chavan.

items.what: Anti-defection bill introduced in the 5th Lok Sabha (Home Minister Uma Shankar Dikshit, Indira Gandhi government)
items.detail: It lapsed when the 5th Lok Sabha was dissolved (1977). It was never passed.

items.what: Another anti-defection bill (Law Minister Shanti Bhushan, Janata government of Morarji Desai)
items.detail: It also failed. It was NOT passed, so it was never 'repealed'.

items.what: 52nd Amendment Act adds the Tenth Schedule
items.detail: Passed unanimously by both Houses. Rajiv Gandhi called it the 'first step towards cleaning-up public life'.

items.what: 91st Amendment Act removes the 'split' exception and caps the size of ministries

blocks.text: For other grounds of disqualification of MPs and MLAs (Art 102 and Art 191), see the Parliament and State Legislature cards.

head: Type of member
Disqualified when
Note
rows: Member of a political party (elected on its ticket)
(a) he voluntarily gives up membership of the party; OR (b) he votes, or stays away from voting (abstains), against the party's direction (whip) without prior permission
For (b): he is not disqualified if the party condones (forgives) the act within 15 days. For (a): a formal resignation is NOT needed; his conduct is enough to show it (Ravi S. Naik case, 1994).
Independent member (elected without any party's ticket)
He joins any political party after the election
There is no grace period. Even after 2 years, joining a party means disqualification.
He joins a political party after 6 months from the day he takes his seat
He may join a party within the first 6 months without losing the seat.

blocks.title: Where the Constitution links to it
items: Art 102(2): an MP disqualified under the Tenth Schedule loses membership of Parliament.
Art 191(2): an MLA or MLC (member of a State Legislative Assembly or Council) disqualified under the Tenth Schedule loses membership of the State Legislature.

The Tenth Schedule does not apply to the election of the President. The Election Commission clarified (July 2017) that parties cannot issue a whip for this election, and voting or not voting in it cannot lead to disqualification.

A whip is the party's direction to its members on attendance and on how to vote in the House. Disobeying it in the House (without permission, and not condoned within 15 days) can lead to disqualification.

sections.heading: Exceptions: when a member is NOT disqualified

head: Exception
Rule
Why
rows: A member is not disqualified if he leaves his party because it merges with another party. A merger counts only when at least two-thirds of the members of the legislature party (the members of that party sitting in the House) agree.
A member elected Speaker, Deputy Speaker, Chairman or Deputy Chairman may give up his party, and may rejoin it after leaving that office. He is not disqualified either time.
Keeps the office impartial and dignified. It does NOT cover the Leader of the Opposition.
Earlier, paragraph 3 of the Tenth Schedule protected a group of one-third of a legislature party that broke away as a 'split'.
Deleted by the 91st Amendment (2003). Today a split gives no protection.

blocks.title: Worked examples
items: Party of 30 members; 12 break away (more than one-third but less than two-thirds). Today they are liable to disqualification, because only a two-thirds merger is protected.
The Schedule does not define 'split' or 'merger' in detail, and gives no time-limit for decisions.

head: House
Who decides defection cases
blocks.note: It is NOT decided by the President, the Governor, the Election Commission or a court.

blocks.title: Defection vs other disqualifications
head: Aspect
Defection (Tenth Schedule)
Other grounds, e.g. office of profit (Art 102(1), 191(1))
rows: President (for MPs, Art 103) or Governor (for state legislators, Art 192)
The President or Governor must act on the opinion of the Election Commission

blocks.title: Procedure (under rules made by the presiding officer)

steps.detail: A case starts only on a written complaint from a member of the House. The presiding officer cannot start it on his own (suo motu).
The member accused gets a chance to explain.
The presiding officer may send the matter to the Committee of Privileges for inquiry.
The presiding officer decides. So a member does not lose the seat immediately or automatically on defecting; it needs this decision.
Decision can be challenged in the High Court or Supreme Court (Kihoto Hollohan case (1992)).

blocks.title: Rule-making power
items: The presiding officer makes rules to carry out the Tenth Schedule (for example, the Members of Lok Sabha (Disqualification on Ground of Defection) Rules, 1985 and the Members of Rajya Sabha (Disqualification on Ground of Defection) Rules, 1985).
The rules must be placed before the House for 30 days. The House may approve, modify or disapprove them.
A wilful breach of these rules by a member may be treated as a breach of privilege of the House.

head: Provision
What it says
rows: Union Council of Ministers, including the Prime Minister, cannot exceed 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
An MP disqualified for defection cannot be appointed a Minister until his term ends or he is re-elected, whichever is earlier.
State Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, cannot exceed 15% of the total strength of the Legislative Assembly. But it cannot have fewer than 12 members.
A member of a State Legislature disqualified for defection cannot be appointed a Minister until his term ends or he is re-elected, whichever is earlier.
A legislator disqualified for defection cannot hold any 'remunerative political post' (a paid government office, or a paid office in a body owned by government) for the same period.

blocks.title: Quick checks
items: Assembly of 60 members: 15% is 9, but the minimum is 12. So the minimum Council of Ministers is 12.
The NCRWC (National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution, 2002) suggested a 10% cap. Parliament chose 15%.
The 91st Amendment did NOT fix the maximum strength of a state ministry at 12. 12 is the minimum.

head: Case (year)
Held
Why it matters
rows: Paragraph 7 (which barred courts from hearing defection cases) was struck down. Because it took away the power of the Supreme Court and High Courts, it needed ratification (approval) by half the states under Art 368(2), and it did not get it. The rest of the Schedule was upheld, because paragraph 7 could be cut away from it (severable).

The presiding officer acts as a tribunal (a body that decides disputes like a court). So courts can review his decision on grounds like mala fides (bad faith), perversity (a decision no reasonable person could reach) and breach of natural justice (for example, not hearing the member). Giving him the power to decide is NOT itself invalid.
Ravi S. Naik vs Union of India (1994)
'Voluntarily giving up membership' can be inferred from conduct, e.g. meeting the Governor with the opposition to withdraw support.
G. Viswanathan vs Speaker, Tamil Nadu (1996)
A member expelled by his party stays counted as a member of that party (an 'unattached' member). If he joins another party, he is deemed to have voluntarily given up membership.
Rajendra Singh Rana vs Swami Prasad Maurya (2007)

The Speaker's failure to decide a disqualification petition, while accepting a claim of 'split' without proof, was an error that the court could correct. The Court itself declared 13 BSP MLAs of Uttar Pradesh disqualified.
Speaker cannot sit on petitions or accept claims blindly.
Upheld the disqualification of 17 Karnataka MLAs, but struck down the part of the Speaker's order barring them from contesting elections until the end of the Assembly's term.
Keisham Meghachandra Singh vs Speaker, Manipur (2020)
A Speaker should ordinarily decide a disqualification petition within 3 months.
This time-limit comes from the court, not from the Tenth Schedule.
Subhash Desai vs Principal Secretary, Governor of Maharashtra (2023)

The whip must be appointed by the political party, not by the legislature party (the group of its members in the House). The Governor's call for a floor test was unjustified. But the earlier government was not restored, because the Chief Minister (Uddhav Thackeray) had resigned without facing the floor test.
Court did not itself disqualify anyone; it left the pending petitions to the Speaker.
Padi Kaushik Reddy vs State of Telangana (31 July 2025)
The Telangana Speaker was told to decide disqualification petitions against 10 BRS (Bharat Rashtra Samithi) MLAs, who had moved to the Congress, within 3 months.

blocks.title: Notable disqualifications
items: Lalduhoma (Mizoram), 1988: first Lok Sabha member disqualified under the law.
4 December 2017: Sharad Yadav and Ali Anwar (JD(U)) disqualified from the Rajya Sabha by Chairman M. Venkaiah Naidu.

blocks.title: Advantages
items: More stability: legislators cannot easily change parties.
Allows regrouping of parties through merger.
Less corruption, and less money spent on frequent, irregular elections.
Political parties got clear constitutional recognition for the first time.

blocks.title: Criticism
items: Does not separate dissent from defection. A member voting against the whip, even on a matter of conscience, can be disqualified. It curbs freedom of dissent.
'Bans retail defection but legalises wholesale defection' (Madhu Limaye): individuals are punished, but groups escape through merger.
It does not provide for a party expelling a legislator for his activities outside the House.
Unfair difference: an independent who joins a party is disqualified, but a nominated member may join a party within 6 months.
Presiding officer may not be impartial and may lack legal knowledge. Lok Sabha Speakers Rabi Ray (1991) and Shivraj Patil (1993) themselves doubted their suitability.

blocks.title: Reform suggestions
head: Body (year)
Recommendation on defection
rows: Disqualification to be decided by the President or Governor on the Election Commission's advice; delete the 'split' exception

Delete the exceptions for both splits and mergers; treat a pre-poll alliance (parties that join together before the election) as one party; disqualification to be decided by the President or Governor on the Election Commission's advice, not by the Speaker

Defectors (individually or in groups) to resign and seek fresh election; to be barred from minister's post or any paid political post for the rest of the term; defector's vote to topple a government to be invalid; power to decide to go to the Election Commission; cap ministers at 10%
Disqualification to be decided by the President or Governor on the Election Commission's advice (to avoid delays)

items: 52nd Amendment 1985 added it; 91st Amendment 2003 amended it. Not 44th, 53rd or 61st.
Split (one-third) protection is gone since 2003. Only a merger with two-thirds consent is protected.
An independent member who joins any party is disqualified. A nominated member may join a party within 6 months of taking his seat.
Speaker or Chairman decides, not the President or Governor. A case starts only on a member's complaint.
The Tenth Schedule has no time-limit. The 3-month rule is from the Keisham Meghachandra case (2020).
Kihoto Hollohan struck down only paragraph 7 (the bar on courts), not the whole Schedule.
Ministries are capped at 15% of the Lok Sabha or Assembly strength, and a state ministry must have at least 12 members. The NCRWC had suggested 10%.
Venkatasubbaiah, not Dinesh Goswami, moved the first resolution in 1967.

Do not mix up amendments: 44th (1978) put 'armed rebellion' in place of 'internal disturbance' in Art 352; 61st (1988, also under Rajiv Gandhi) lowered the voting age from 21 to 18; 101st (2016) brought GST.

Do not mix up cases: Kihoto Hollohan (1992) is the defection case; S.R. Bommai (1994) is about floor test and President's Rule; Kuldip Nayar (2006) upheld open ballot in Rajya Sabha polls; PUCL (2013) gave NOTA; ADR (2024) struck down electoral bonds.

Vijay's party, Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), won 108 of 234 seats — 10 short of the 118 needed for a majority. Congress, CPI, CPI(M) and VCK (Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi) had fought the election against TVK, but supported it after the results
An example of a post-poll alliance (alliance made after the results). Vijay became Chief Minister on 10 May 2026 — the first government in Tamil Nadu led by a non-Dravidian party in about six decades

blocks.title: Leader of the Opposition — rule
items: For its leader to be recognised as Leader of the Opposition, a party must have at least one-tenth (10%) of the total strength of the House. In the Lok Sabha that means 55 members (not 75).

blocks.title: Laxmikanth's four kinds of regional parties

Formed by a split in a national party — e.g. Biju Janata Dal, RJD (Rashtriya Janata Dal), Trinamool Congress, YSR Congress

items: Sukumar Sen was the first CEC; K.V.K. Sundaram was the longest-serving; R.V.S. Peri Sastri was the first Telugu CEC; V.S. Ramadevi was the first woman CEC; T.N. Seshan was the 10th CEC.
Gyanesh Kumar is the 26th CEC (from 19 February 2025). Rajiv Kumar retired and is no longer in the Commission.
The 2019 election formed the 17th Lok Sabha; the 2024 election formed the 18th Lok Sabha.
The 2024 schedule was announced on 16 March 2024, not 20 February. Vote-from-home was for voters aged 85 and above and for disabled voters — not for women.
The BJP won 303 seats in 2019 but only 240 in 2024, so in 2024 it had no majority on its own.
The largest opposition party in the first Lok Sabha was the CPI, not the Swatantra Party. The TDP was the largest opposition party after the 1984 election.
A Leader of the Opposition needs the party to hold 10% of the House strength (55 in the Lok Sabha), not 75. The first official Leader of the Opposition was recognised in 1969.
Order of milestones: decision to issue EPIC (photo identity cards) in 1993, then EVMs in all Lok Sabha seats in 2004, then NOTA in 2013.
